title: Je veux juste voir Mathias  (I Just Want to See Mathias)

segments.t: Now a stranger walks in. Camille is in her early twenties, new to Paris from the south of France, and she goes straight to the reception desk, where Sofia is juggling the phones. She wants to see Mathias, and she has no appointment. First the whole thing in French; you don't need to catch every word.
Soit jeudi à quatorze heures, soit vendredi à onze heures.
Bonjour.
Bonjour. Je peux vous aider?
Je suis là pour voir Mathias Barneville.
Il vous attend?
Non, mais c'est important.
Laissez vos photos et votre CV ici.
Cette agence ne représente que des stars.
Je ne suis pas actrice. Je veux juste voir Mathias.
Votre nom?
Camille Valentini. Il me connaît.
Sans rendez-vous? Je ne promets rien.
Asseyez-vous.
Merci.
Mathias, Camille Valentini est là. Désolée de vous déranger.
Let's walk through it. When Camille arrives, Sofia is still on the phone, offering somebody two possible meeting times.
Soit jeudi à quatorze heures, soit vendredi à onze heures.
'Either Thursday at two, or Friday at eleven.' The same little word, said twice, gives you 'either, or'. And two in the afternoon is fourteen hours again, office style.
Bonjour.
'Hello.' Camille waits politely for her turn.
Je peux vous aider?
'Can I help you?' Sofia uses the formal 'you', the right choice with a stranger at a front desk.
Je suis là pour voir Mathias Barneville.
'I'm here to see Mathias Barneville.' The little word meaning 'to' or 'in order to' links 'here' to the plain verb 'to see'. Camille uses his full name, like a visitor would.
Il vous attend?
'Is he expecting you?' Literally 'he waits for you'. The formal 'you' sits before the verb.
Non, mais c'est important.
'No, but it's important.' Short and firm. Sofia has seen this many times before.
Laissez vos photos et votre CV ici.
'Leave your photos and your CV here.' A polite command, with the formal ending. She is sure Camille is one more young actress hoping to be discovered.
Cette agence ne représente que des stars.
'This agency only represents stars.' Here's a neat trick: the negative pair is used with a different second word, and the meaning becomes 'only'. Nothing but stars.
Je ne suis pas actrice.
'I'm not an actress.' The ordinary negative this time, wrapped around the verb 'to be'. And with jobs, French drops the word for 'a'.
Je veux juste voir Mathias.
'I just want to see Mathias.' Now she uses only his first name, which tells Sofia something.
Votre nom?
'Your name?' Half a question, all business.
Il me connaît.
'He knows me.' The word for 'me' comes before the verb. Sofia is not convinced.
Sans rendez-vous? Je ne promets rien.
'Without an appointment? I'm not promising anything.' The negative again, this time with the word for 'nothing'.
Asseyez-vous.
'Have a seat.' Literally 'sit yourself down', a polite command you'll hear in any waiting room.
Merci.
'Thank you.' Camille sits down and waits.
Mathias, Camille Valentini est là.
'Mathias, Camille Valentini is here.' Sofia rings through to his office.
Désolée de vous déranger.

'Sorry to bother you.' Sofia apologises to her boss, so she uses the formal 'you' with him too. And the name works: Mathias agrees to see this young woman with no appointment. Here's the whole scene again. Now listen to the whole conversation one more time.
Soit jeudi à quatorze heures, soit vendredi à onze heures.
Bonjour.
Bonjour. Je peux vous aider?
Je suis là pour voir Mathias Barneville.
Il vous attend?
Non, mais c'est important.
Laissez vos photos et votre CV ici.
Cette agence ne représente que des stars.
Je ne suis pas actrice. Je veux juste voir Mathias.
Votre nom?
Camille Valentini. Il me connaît.
Sans rendez-vous? Je ne promets rien.
Asseyez-vous.
Merci.
Mathias, Camille Valentini est là. Désolée de vous déranger.
You've just learned how to ask for someone at a front desk, and how to say you only want one thing. See you next time!
Merci, au revoir!
